title: A rover brain made of gates
instruction: Build the robot’s decision-making from logic gates, without a single line of program. The inputs are sensors (1 = sees the line or has bumped into something), the outputs are motors and actions (1 = running). You get a star for the smallest number of gates.

levels.story: The rover has two line sensors, L and P. On a straight both see the line, in a bend only one. Connect the motors ML and MP so that the rover turns towards the line. When only the right motor runs, it turns left.
levels.why: You don’t need any gate: connect ML to P and MP to L. Crossed wires are the whole program. This is called a Braitenberg vehicle.

levels.story: When the line disappears (L = 0 and P = 0), the rover shouldn’t stop, but turn right until it finds it. The other rows stay as before.
levels.why: ML should be 1 in three rows out of four, and 0 only for L = 1, P = 0. That kind of “almost always” is easy to build from OR: ML = NOT L OR P.

levels.story: A robot vacuum has two bumpers, L and P. When either one hits something, it should back up (C). It should turn right (V) only when only the left one has hit something.
levels.why: C = L OR P. For V you need L and at the same time not P: one NOT and one AND. When both bumpers hit, it backs up straight.

levels.story: The rover has got a third sensor in the middle, S. When the middle sees the line, it goes straight. When only a side sensor sees it, it turns towards that sensor. When none sees anything, it stops. At a crossroads, where both side sensors see the line, it also goes straight.
levels.why: Each motor listens to the middle and the opposite side: ML = S OR P, MP = S OR L. Eight rows of the table and only two gates.

levels.story: In the corridor by the workshop there are two switches, A downstairs and B upstairs. Every click switches the light S, whichever switch you click. But the XOR gates have run out.
levels.why: The light is on when exactly one switch is on: (A OR B) AND NOT (A AND B). Four gates. That’s why XOR is made as a part of its own.

debrief: You can build a robot’s decision table from gates. Grey Walter’s tortoises, some of the first robots from the late 1940s, had only a few valves and behaved as if they were thinking. A program in the micro:bit does the same, except you can rewrite it without soldering.
